reader_questions.q: What makes France’s debt situation a crisis now, rather than simply a high level of public debt?
How large are France’s debt, annual deficit and interest bill relative to its economy, its own history and comparable countries?
reader_questions.where: The opening snapshot, “The deficit also has a revenue side” and “Repeated gaps accumulate into debt” give debt and deficit levels and historical comparisons; the interest bill and international comparisons are missing.

reader_questions.q: What has driven the debt problem, and how much comes from spending, taxation, weak growth or higher borrowing costs?
reader_questions.where: “Bigger bills, but not always a bigger share of the economy” and “The deficit also has a revenue side” explain spending composition, indexation and recent revenue weakness, but do not quantify the contributions of growth, tax policy and borrowing costs.

reader_questions.q: What changed, and when, to make investors or policymakers more worried about France’s ability to manage its debt?
How do France’s political constraints and membership of the euro affect its ability to resolve the problem?
Who is affected by the debt crisis, and who would bear the costs of measures to address it?
reader_questions.where: “The biggest commitment is social protection” identifies recipients of public spending, but never connects them, taxpayers or service users to the consequences of the debt problem or proposed remedies.

reader_questions.q: What would have to change to stabilise France’s debt, and what could make the situation materially worse?

missed_findings: The story supplies no dated evidence of financing stress or a loss of policy credibility, so it never establishes whether “crisis” is the right description.

The supplied figures show the deficit widening by 1.1 percentage points of GDP between 2022 and 2024 because revenue fell by 2.5 points while spending fell by 1.4 points; this is the clearest quantified explanation and deserves the lead.
The debt chart shows a 9.5-percentage-point rise between end-2023 and June 2026, a recent reversal that the prose leaves unquantified and unexplained.
The interest bill, its change over time and comparable countries’ fiscal positions are missing, preventing the reader from judging how exceptional or costly France’s position is.
The story omits the political and euro-area constraints on adjustment and the distribution of costs among taxpayers, benefit recipients and public-service users.
No debt-stabilisation calculation connects the primary balance, borrowing costs and nominal growth, leaving the reader without a benchmark for the adjustment required.

charts.shows: Spending exceeded revenue by €153 billion in 2025; receipts covered roughly 91% of spending.
Social protection and health together accounted for 57.1% of public spending in 2024.
Old age accounts for more than half of social protection, with the other benefit categories separately identified.
Social protection grew in euros but declined relative to GDP between 2014 and 2024, alongside longer histories and nine subgroup comparisons.
charts.fix: Remove the nine-category lower panel from the main story so the chart concentrates on the nominal-growth versus GDP-share finding.

charts.shows: Spending exceeded revenue throughout 1995–2025, and revenue fell faster than spending relative to GDP between 2022 and 2024.
charts.fix: Annotate the 2022–2024 movements directly on the lines to make the recent deficit-widening mechanism the visual focus.

charts.shows: The annual deficit narrowed from 5.8% to 5.1% of GDP in 2025 but remained above its 2019 level.
Debt rose over the longer term, fell relative to GDP after 2020, then reached 119% in June 2026.
charts.fix: Highlight the 9.5-percentage-point increase since end-2023 to focus attention on the recent deterioration.

top_change: Rebuild the story around whether and why France faces a debt crisis now, leading with dated evidence of fiscal or financing pressure and explaining why political constraints, growth and borrowing costs make stabilisation difficult; compress the spending inventory to supporting context.

lessons.rule: Answer the commissioned question in the opening claim, and use descriptive breakdowns only where they advance that answer.
lessons.evidence: The commission asks why there is a debt crisis; the title and opening instead ask where public money goes.

lessons.rule: Distinguish a large debt stock from a current crisis using dated evidence of financing conditions or policy constraints.
lessons.evidence: The story reports debt of 119% of GDP without showing investor concern, a policy trigger or an inability to finance spending.

lessons.rule: Separate spending levels from explanations of changes in the deficit.
lessons.evidence: Social protection dominates the budget, but the 2022–2024 deficit deterioration occurred while spending fell relative to GDP and revenue fell further.

lessons.rule: Preserve counter-evidence and distinguish nominal amounts from economic burdens.
lessons.evidence: The story correctly retains the 2025 deficit improvement and explains why a 31% nominal increase in social protection can accompany a declining GDP share.

lessons.rule: Give each chart one principal finding and reserve detailed inventories for supporting material.
lessons.evidence: The evolution figure combines aggregate histories, nine subgroup comparisons and nominal-growth accounting in one visual block.

argument.why: The coherent argument about spending composition and revenue does not answer the commissioned question about why France faces a debt crisis.

depth.why: Attributed explanations of revenue weakness and indexation challenge a simple welfare-spending account, but the central questions about crisis timing and debt sustainability remain unexplained.

charts.why: The charts are labelled, sourced and generally well matched to their data, but the evolution figure carries several points and the collection mainly supports a spending explainer.

honesty.why: The supplied figures are internally consistent, sources and vintages are identified, causal explanations are attributed, and limits concerning nominal growth, revisions and default prediction are explicit.

reader_questions.why: Four questions are unanswered, including why this is a crisis now; the remaining three receive only partial answers.

prose.why: Most sentences are plain and specific, but accounting-category explanations consume scarce space while “cycle-adjusted assessment” and “taxable bases” receive insufficient explanation.
